text.p: The following are the main stories from Thursday morning's Austrian newspapers:
- Savings banks want to reach a compromise with the EU over anonymous accounts. They favour leaving existing accounts intact but preventing the opening of new ones.
- President Thomas Klestil will stand as candidate for a second year in office, according to sources close to him.
- Chamber of Labour head Herbert Tumpel demands new measures to increase job security. He says flexible working hours alone are not enough.
- Bank Austria deputy chief executive Karl Samstag has reassured Creditanstalt shareholders that it will make them an attractive offer to exchange their shares.
- Coffee, Austria's favourite drink, will be more expensive from March.
- The Social Democrats may support People's Party candidate Thomas Klestil if he runs for a second term as president, a spokesman for Social Democrat Chancellor Viktor Klima said.

- The coalition government has agreed on media laws that will finally liberalise the market. The draft allows cable television stations to operate without a licence and clears the way for 55 private radio stations.
- From Thursday, Austria is increasing the number of soldiers guarding the border with Hungary in preparation for Schengen.
- Austria faces a big fine if it loses a legal argument with the EU over anonymous savings accounts.
- 10,200 employees were on short-time working in 1996, compared with 3,700 in 1995. Costs for short-time working rose to 63 million schillings from 21.4 million.
- A third GSM mobile telephone licence could be awarded as early as July.
- Bank Austria deputy chief executive Karl Samstag said Austria has 500 bank branches too many.
- Job security has a price. Flexible working hours could lead to a loss in income of up to 20 percent in branches where employees work a lot of overtime.
- Finance Minister Rudolf Edlinger wants to reform Austrian taxation.
